clue.text: Scolded unruly babies

indicators.note: unruly things refuse to stay in order, so the preceding word's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone told off some badly behaved infants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'babies' looks like a noun for the unruly infants, but it is a verb here: to baby someone is to pamper them.
explanation.definitionFit: To baby a person is to treat them overprotectively, which is exactly what pampering or mollycoddling means.

clue.text: Film star's pleasure trips on ships

blocks.note: first meaning: belonging to Tom Cruise, the Hollywood actor
second meaning: holiday voyages on liners

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive of the actor's surname looks the same, without its apostrophe, as the plural of the holiday voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Cruise is a film star, so his possessive matches; cruises are also leisure voyages by sea.

clue.text: State education set up by county in Ireland

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the word is raised, reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: ED is the abbreviation for education
Clare is a county on Ireland's west coast

explanation.surface: State schooling is established by an Irish county council.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like an adjective (state education), but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To state something is to say it formally, which is to declare it.

clue.text: Hat keeps one very, very angry

indicators.note: keeps means holds inside, so the following pieces sit within the hat

blocks.note: lid is slang for a hat
I is the Roman numeral one and V abbreviates very

explanation.surface: A hat-wearer is incandescent with rage.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'very' is wordplay and the second belongs to the definition, very angry.
explanation.definitionFit: Livid means furious, so it describes someone extremely cross rather than merely annoyed.

clue.text: Shocked sips with ruder drunk

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prim drinker is appalled by the manners of a coarser, drunken companion.
explanation.definitionFit: Being surprised is being taken aback, a milder synonym of shocked.

clue.text: This could make cats rejected

indicators.note: the clue asks what could produce the word cats, pointing to a rearrangement read in reverse

blocks.note: a rearrangement of the letters of cats
the second half of the solution is itself a common anagram signal, so the whole answer reads as an instruction that turns one word into cats

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark about something that could get cats spurned.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read CAST OFF as wordplay, with OFF as the anagram signal, and CAST 'off' makes CATS.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast-off item is one discarded or thrown away by its owner, the same as rejected.

clue.text: Garments Charlie put on chimpanzees?

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
chimpanzees are apes

explanation.surface: Charlie dresses some chimps in clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' reads as dressing the apes, but it only joins the letter to the word it is set before.
explanation.definitionFit: Capes are sleeveless cloaks, a type of clothing, so the plural fits garments.

clue.text: Allows penalties

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, gives official permission for
second meaning: a noun, punitive measures imposed on a country

explanation.walkthrough: The word is a contronym: as a verb it permits, as a plural noun it punishes.
explanation.definitionFit: To sanction is to authorise or approve, while sanctions are also punitive restrictions such as trade embargoes.

clue.text: Run over and gabble about latest bit of nonsense

indicators.note: about places one word around the selected letter
the latest bit is the final piece, so take the last letter of the following word

blocks.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for an over
to prate is to chatter foolishly
the final letter of nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone talks gibberish at length and finishes by spouting nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: E sits inside PRATE, after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: To run a machine or business is to operate it, a straight synonym.

clue.text: The woman's following stout clergymen

indicators.note: following says the piece before it in the clue comes after the next one in the answer

blocks.note: stout means fat
something belonging to a woman is hers

explanation.surface: A woman is walking behind some portly priests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' places the woman's word after the stout one; stout also tempts as the dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Catholic priests are addressed as Father, so fathers are clergymen.

clue.text: Reveal new cavern in ancient city

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the following word

blocks.note: Ur was an ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia
N is the standard abbreviation for new
a cove can be a cave or sheltered recess in a cliff

explanation.surface: An archaeologist announces a fresh cave discovered at an old site.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur, in ancient Mesopotamia, is the crossword's favourite ancient city; a cove can be a cave as well as a bay.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncover something is to expose or disclose it, a direct synonym of reveal.

clue.text: Biting half of orange in boat

indicators.note: half of asks for just three of the six letters of the following word, here the back three
in places the selected letters inside the vessel that follows

blocks.note: a punt is a flat-bottomed river boat
the latter half of the word orange

explanation.surface: Someone bites into a piece of orange while out in a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Either half of orange is possible; only the back half fits the boat. A punt is a flat-bottomed boat pushed with a pole.
explanation.definitionFit: A pungent smell or remark is sharp and stinging, which is what biting describes.

clue.text: Put up with poets with no British qualities

indicators.note: with no says the following letter is to be removed from the word before it

blocks.note: to stand something is to tolerate it
bards are poets
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: Someone tolerates verse-writers who lack British character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' appears twice: the first belongs to 'Put up with', the second merely links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Standards are levels of quality or excellence, so the plural noun matches qualities as a loose synonym.

clue.text: Drinks with English guy

blocks.note: cups of tea are drinks
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Having drinks alongside an Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guy' looks like a man, but it is the verb: to guy someone is to mock them.
explanation.definitionFit: To guy someone is an old verb meaning to ridicule or make fun of, which is what teasing does.

clue.text: Mini blocking street? Charming!

indicators.note: something blocking a road sits across it, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
wee is a Scottish word for tiny

explanation.surface: A Mini car parked across a street draws a sarcastic 'Charming!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mini' suggests the car, but here it just means small. The exclamation lets 'Charming!' work as an interjection.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet and charming are both everyday words for something delightful, and both serve as exclamations.

clue.text: Keen fish swallowing river insect

indicators.note: a fish swallowing something takes it inside, so one piece goes within the fish

blocks.note: a tench is a freshwater fish
R is the abbreviation for river
an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: An eager fish gulps down a river insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' reads as eager, but it is the sharp sense: a keen blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen can mean sharp or cutting, and trenchant criticism is incisive and cutting.

clue.text: Around end of November, son chose new glasses

indicators.note: end of asks for the final letter of the word that follows
new suggests the preceding words are made into something fresh, so their letters are rearranged
around says the rearranged letters wrap themselves round the selected letter

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
the final letter of November

explanation.surface: Late in November a boy picked out some new spectacles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'glasses' points to spectacles, but schooners are tall drinking glasses for sherry or beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is a tall drinking vessel, so the plural is a kind of glasses.

clue.text: Raunchier, volatile old fighter

indicators.note: something volatile is unstable and changeable, so the preceding letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A retired boxer has become racier and more temperamental.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old fighter' suggests a boxer, but it is the Hawker Hurricane, a British fighter plane of the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hawker Hurricane was a Battle of Britain aircraft, an example of a vintage fighter plane.

clue.text: Let go of nurse with red pants and run

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are poorly arranged and must be reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A nurse wearing red trousers releases something and flees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like trousers (or panting), but in British slang it means rubbish, signalling a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To surrender something is to give it up or relinquish it, which is to let go of it.

clue.text: Pop star embracing sex appeal, posing

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold inside one's arms, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: Sting is the singer from The Police
it is old slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A rock singer is hugging a sexy model during a photoshoot.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitting for a portrait means posing for the artist, so the two words share that sense.

clue.text: Snake? Some feel it perhaps climbing

indicators.note: some means only a portion, so the answer lies inside the run of following words
in a down clue, climbing means reading upwards, from end to start

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning feel it perhaps

explanation.surface: A snake is perhaps felt climbing up something.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition by example: a snake is one kind of this creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A snake is a scaly cold-blooded creature, an example of the wider class named by the answer.

clue.text: Golfer's unhappy round ended oddly abandoned

indicators.note: abandoning the odd letters leaves only the even ones of the preceding word
round says one word goes around the selected letters

blocks.note: sad means unhappy
the second and fourth letters of ended

explanation.surface: A golfer is miserable because a round finished with shots thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: Sam Snead was an American golfer who won a record 82 PGA Tour events.
explanation.definitionFit: Sam Snead is a famous American professional golfer, so he is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Mountain most harsh when leaving summit

indicators.note: the summit is the top, so in a down entry the opening letter departs

blocks.note: severest is the superlative of severe

explanation.surface: A climber finds a mountain hardest while coming down from the top.
explanation.walkthrough: SEVEREST drops its first S.
explanation.definitionFit: Everest is the highest mountain on Earth, so it is an example of a mountain.

clue.text: Wanted gentleman confined by legal document

indicators.note: something confined is held inside, so the first word goes within the second

blocks.note: a deed is a legal document
sir is the title for a gentleman

explanation.surface: A wanted man is bound by a court order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanted' suggests a criminal on the run, but it just means longed for.
explanation.definitionFit: Desired means wished for, a direct synonym of the past tense wanted.

clue.text: Sign of nerves about work issue

indicators.note: about places one word around the other

blocks.note: a tic is a nervous twitch
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A nervous twitch caused by a problem at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work issue' reads as a workplace problem, but 'issue' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is a subject under discussion, a matter, which is what a topic is.

clue.text: 25 per cent of students poorly? Head's calm

indicators.note: a quarter of an eight-letter word is its opening two letters

blocks.note: the opening quarter of students
poorly means ill
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: A quarter of the pupils are sick, but the headmaster stays calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' suggests a head teacher, but a ness is a promontory.
explanation.definitionFit: Stillness is a state of quiet and lack of motion, which is the noun sense of calm.

clue.text: Promise sailors initially we are docked

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the preceding word
a docked tail is cut short, so the last letter is cut off

blocks.note: the first letter of sailors
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sailors pledge they have arrived in port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' looks like a ship mooring, but it means cut short: WE ARE loses its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: To swear is to vow or give one's solemn word, which is to promise.

clue.text: Holiday? Pack your bags!

blocks.note: first meaning: a noun, time off work
second meaning: an imperative, go away

explanation.walkthrough: The pairing makes it sound like getting ready for a holiday, but the second phrase is an order to depart.
explanation.definitionFit: Leave is time off granted from work, a holiday; and 'leave!' commands someone to go, as 'pack your bags!' does.

clue.text: Parrot's wild – I tame it

indicators.note: something wild is untamed and disordered, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An owner boasts of taming an unruly parrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parrot' looks like the bird, but it is the verb: to repeat what others say.
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot is to copy someone's words mechanically, which is to mimic them.

clue.text: Unskilful friend consumed by gold fever, ultimately

indicators.note: something consumed is taken inside, so one piece goes within the other
ultimately points to the last letter of the preceding word

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a mate is a friend
the final letter of fever

explanation.surface: A clumsy friend gripped by gold fever in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateur can be an adjective meaning inexpert or unprofessional, which matches unskilful.

clue.text: Bigger kitchen tool, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word is identified by how it is pronounced, not spelt

blocks.note: a grater shreds cheese or vegetables in the kitchen

explanation.surface: Someone describes a larger kitchen utensil.
explanation.definitionFit: Greater is the comparative of great, meaning larger, a straight synonym of bigger.

clue.text: Dispirited wanting leader thrown out

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: dejected means downcast or dispirited

explanation.surface: A downhearted person without a captain is expelled.
explanation.walkthrough: DEJECTED loses its first letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ejected is to be expelled or forcibly removed, so it means thrown out.
